name: Staging — Building Pleasure Through Phases
summary: Sex isn't a linear path—what feels good changes minute by minute within a single session. Jumping straight to the clitoris tends to create small, quick orgasms; building gradually through defined stages produces more intense ones. What feels comfortable one moment can feel painful the next as the body changes.
detailed_description: OMGYES frames arousal as a series of blended stages rather than sharp steps: building desire/warmup, warmup transition, build-up, approach, orgasm, and rebuild/multiple orgasm. Transitions usually aren't clean boundaries—they blend, so feedback matters to know when to change pressure, pace, or focus. A key physical insight: before arousal, direct clitoral touch can hurt; once fully aroused, the clit enlarges and emerges and now wants pressure rather than avoidance. Matching touch to the current stage is what drives intensity.
stepwise_structure: 1. Start slow and away from the clit; build desire before direct genital touch.
2. Transition gradually onto the clit, easing pressure up rather than full force at first contact.
3. In build-up, experiment with subtle detail changes to find what escalates pleasure.
4. On approach, lock onto one working motion and hold it consistently.
5. Through orgasm, keep the motion or adjust intensity to preference.
6. After orgasm, move lightly through the oversensitive phase before rebuilding.
safety_notes: Pre-arousal direct clitoral touch can hurt—warm up first.
Post-orgasm oversensitivity needs gentle, light contact, not immediate pressure.
Read verbal and nonverbal feedback; the same motion can feel good then wrong as the body changes.
Adults in consensual contexts only; not a substitute for professional care.

meta.physical_changes_note: During arousal the vulva becomes red and puffy and the clit enlarges and emerges; touch that hurts when unaroused is often wanted (with pressure) when fully aroused.
meta.what_partners_often_miss: Vulvas are not an on/off switch like a penis; sensitivity changes constantly, so timing matters as much as technique.
meta.transitions_note: Stages blend into one another rather than switching sharply; ask for feedback to track changes.
